Q: C++ use of std::move for return of rvalue function parameter? A:

That rule is slightly incomplete except when "local" also includes "function parameters". Function parameters are move-eligible, and the compiler will apply move semantics automatically. While the std::move doesn't hurt by today's rules, it is still unnecessary and unexpected.

Q: Tkinter frame changes with buttons A:

If you want to make it full screen then you need

window.attributes("-fullscreen", True)

You can also make it top most to display it above other windows in system

window.attributes("-topmost", True)

(on Linux I need it to force "fullscreen" to display it above other windows)

but this may block access to other windows and makes problem to debug code when there is mistake - and it may need to add also "-topmost", False after "-topmost", True (at least on Linux I need it)

But I see few problems with all this code.

  1. you have function ready_to_change() and local variable ready_to_change in some functions - but you need global variable ready_to_change to access value in both places. But this can makes conflict with function ready_to_change(). You should have two different names and variable has to be global. But frankly, I don't understand what for you need this variable.

  2. GUI frameworks don't work like command input() because GUI has to check keyboard and mouse (all time) and update widgets when you move mouse. And Tkinter has mainloop which all time runs loop which checks keys, mouse, events and redraw widgets. So welcome() ready_to_change() and frame_change() don't wait for user's decisions. They are executed before you even see window (which is displayed when mainloop() is executed). If you want to change frame then you have to do it directly in function assigned to button command=ready_to_change

  3. there is other problem - menu_frame doesn't exists when you run frame_change(welcome_frame, menu_frame) because it is created when you run menu(). It would need to create menu_frame at start without running menu_frame.pack() and later you can use .pack() to display it.

  4. if frame was displayed with .pack() then you should use .pack_forget() instead of .place_forget(). Functions .pack(), .place() and .grid() are different "layout managers" which calculate widgets positions in different way.

Full working code

import tkinter as tk

# --- constansts --- # PEP8: `UPPER_CASE_NAMES`

COLOR = "#304671"

# --- functions ---


def frame_change(old_frame, new_frame):
    old_frame.pack_forget()
    new_frame.pack(expand=True)


def change_welcome_to_menu():
    window.attributes("-fullscreen", True)
    window.attributes("-topmost", True)    # force window to display at top
    window.attributes("-topmost", False)  # if you still want access to other windows in system
    frame_change(welcome_frame, menu_frame)


def create_welcome_frame(window):

    welcome_frame = tk.Frame(window, bg=COLOR, bd=16)

    welcome_message_txt = """
    Welcome to
    Dungeon RPG
    """
    welcome_message = tk.Label(
        welcome_frame,
        text=welcome_message_txt,
        font=("dragonfly", 50),
        bg=COLOR,
        fg="white",
    )
    welcome_message.pack()

    welcome_end_button = tk.Button(
        welcome_frame,
        text="Continue",
        font=("dragonfly", 20),
        bg=COLOR,
        fg="white",
        command=change_welcome_to_menu,
    )
    welcome_end_button.pack()

    # without `welcome_frame.pack(expand=True)`

    return welcome_frame


def create_menu_frame(window):

    menu_frame = tk.Frame(window, bg=COLOR, bd=16)

    menu_label = tk.Label(
        menu_frame, text="DungeonRPG", font=("dragonfly", 35), bg=COLOR, fg="white"
    )
    menu_label.pack()

    menu_end_button = tk.Button(
        menu_frame,
        text="Close",
        font=("dragonfly", 20),
        bg=COLOR,
        fg="white",
        command=window.destroy,
    )
    menu_end_button.pack()

    # without `menu_frame.pack(expand=True)`

    return menu_frame


# --- main ---

window = tk.Tk()
window.title("Dungeon RPG")
# window.geometry("1x1")
window.config(background=COLOR)

# create all frames without displaying
welcome_frame = create_welcome_frame(window)
menu_frame = create_menu_frame(window)

# display welcome_frame as first frame in program
welcome_frame.pack(expand=True)

window.mainloop()

Q: Why does a floating-point multiplication compile more efficiently when I put it in an inline function? A:

All the problems here are caused by "sloppy typing". That is, just carelessly tossing in int instead of a specific integer type, or tossing in double type literals in a program actually working with float. Best practices involve:

  • Never let there be implicit type conversions anywhere in the program.
  • Never use int, use stdint.h types.
  • Never mix float and double in the same expression. Write functions supporting either float or double, not some strange hybrids working with both at once.
  • Never mix operands that are integer and floating point in the same expression either: don't leave it all to be implicit converted. Common source of bugs.
  • Only use float if you actually have a target where 32 bit floating point hardware support is what makes sense, like on a ARM Cortex M that only supports single precision FPUs at best. Otherwise use double.

In the specific code, the compiler can tell that the static version will always have a double constant passed on to a function accepting float, so that conversion can be carried out at compile time. inline has nothing to do with it. If we get rid of the "sloppy typing" then both functions turn 100% equivalent though:

#include <stdint.h>

float Halve1(int32_t a) {return (float)a * (1.0f/2.0f);}

static inline float Mul(float a, float b) {return a * b;}
float Halve2(int32_t a) {return Mul((float)a, 1.0f/2.0f);}

The most significant change being the swap from double to float literals. The explicit casts are mostly just self-documenting code for "hey I actually know what I'm doing here and didn't accidentally leave any implicit type conversions behind to cause potential havoc".

gcc 15.2 ARM32 -O3:

Halve1:
        push    {r4, lr}
        bl      __aeabi_i2f
        mov     r1, #1056964608
        bl      __aeabi_fmul
        pop     {r4, lr}
        bx      lr
Halve2:
        push    {r4, lr}
        bl      __aeabi_i2f
        mov     r1, #1056964608
        bl      __aeabi_fmul
        pop     {r4, lr}
        bx      lr

Gone are the conversions to double.

Q: Spark Declarative Pipelines - How to refresh a materalized view? A:

The issue is that Spark sees the existing folder and doesn't want to overwrite it. Your @materialized_view code is trying to 'build' a new view from scratch, but since the spot is already taken, Spark stops there to keep your data safe.

You have two options:

  1. To update the data: Don't re-run the definition. Just use the Refresh command.

  2. To change the logic: You need to Drop the old view first to clear the spot. Only then will Spark let you create it again.

It's like building a house: if there’s already one on the lot, you either renovate it (Refresh) or tear it down (Drop) before building a new one. You can't just act like the lot is empty

Q: Refactor Stateful/Loop-based approach into Set-based approach A:

You can do it using analytic functions:

WITH calc_index AS (
  -- Give each row an index per campaign so that they are orderable.
  -- Count the number of products per campaign.
  SELECT product_grp_id,
         budget_year,
         campaign_seq_nbr,
         campaign_count,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY product_grp_id, budget_year, campaign_seq_nbr
           ORDER BY NULL
         ) AS campaign_index,
         COUNT(1) OVER (
           PARTITION BY product_grp_id, budget_year, campaign_seq_nbr
         ) AS campaign_product_cnt,
         total_budget
  FROM   marketing_budget_alloc  
),
allocate_to_campaign AS (
  -- Allocate 1 to each campaign within a product group up to the
  -- total budget.
  -- Calculate the total budget for each campaign within the product group.
  SELECT c.*,
         CASE
         WHEN campaign_index = 1
         AND  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                PARTITION BY product_grp_id, budget_year
                ORDER BY campaign_index, campaign_seq_nbr
              ) <= total_budget
         THEN 1
         ELSE 0 
         END AS min_alloc,
         TRUNC( total_budget * campaign_seq_nbr / campaign_count )
         - TRUNC( total_budget * (campaign_seq_nbr - 1) / campaign_count )
         AS total_campaign_budget
  FROM   calc_index c
)
-- Calculate the allocation fraction (not percentage).
-- If there are more campaigns than budget then use the minimum allocation
-- otherwise allocate the campaign budget shares within the product group
-- to each product in the campaign.
SELECT product_grp_id,
       budget_year,
       campaign_seq_nbr,
       campaign_count,
       total_budget,
       TRUNC(campaign_index / campaign_product_cnt, 3)
       - TRUNC(( campaign_index - 1) / campaign_product_cnt, 3)
         AS alloc_pct,
       CASE
       WHEN campaign_count > total_budget
       THEN min_alloc
       ELSE TRUNC(total_campaign_budget * campaign_index / campaign_product_cnt)
            - TRUNC(total_campaign_budget * (campaign_index - 1) / campaign_product_cnt)
       END AS max_alloc
FROM   allocate_to_campaign
ORDER BY
       product_grp_id,
       budget_year,
       campaign_seq_nbr,
       campaign_index

Note: I am calculating alloc_pct as the allocation for individual row in the table as a fraction of the budget for the campaign within the product group/year pairing. This gets the correct values for groups 2 & 4 but I cannot see what logic you have used to get your sample output for the other groups (unless your sample data is wrong and groups 1 and 3 should have each product in a separate campaign - but even then, I can't see any logic for your output for group 5.)

Which, for the sample data (note, your fiddle is missing the final row), outputs:

Q: Is there a difference between "!=" and "is not" in C#? A:

Comparison table:

Operator != is not
Original purpose Value inequality Negated pattern matching
Can perform value inequality Yes Yes
Can perform negated pattern matching No Yes
Can invoke implicit operator on left-hand operand Yes No
Can invoke implicit operator on right-hand operand(s) Yes Yes1
Is its own operator Yes No2
Overloadable Yes No
Since C# 1.0 C# 9.03
Value-type null-comparison branch elision4 Yes No[Citation needed]5
Impossible comparisons Always Errors. Warnings usually, sometimes Errors.
Left operand Any expression Any expression
Right operand(s) Any expression Only constant expressions6
Syntax <any-expr> != <any-expr> `<any-expr> is [not] <const-expr> [or

Common examples:

Example != is not
Not null x != null x is not null
Value inequality example x != 'a' x is not 'a'
Runtime type (mis)match x.GetType() != typeof(Char) x is not Char7
SQL x NOT IN ( 1, 2, 3 ) x != 1 && x != 2 && x != 3 x is not (1 or 2 or 3)8

To answer the OP's question directly and specifically:

if( x != y ) { }
// vs:
if( x is not y ) { }

  • If x is an integral value-type (e.g. int/ Int32) and y is a const-expression (e.g. const int y = 123;) then no, there is no difference, and both statements result in the same .NET MSIL bytecode being generated (both with and without compiler optimizations enabled):

  • If y is a type-name (instead of a value name) then there is a difference: the first if statement is invalid and won't compile, and the if( x is not y ) statement is a type pattern match instead of a constant pattern match.

Footnotes:

  1. "Constant Pattern": "When the input value is not an open type, the constant expression is implicitly converted to the type of the matched expression".

  2. x is not null is more analogous to !(x == null) than x != null.

  3. C# 7.0 introduced some limited forms of constant-pattern matching, which was further expanded by C# 8.0, but it wasn't until C# 9.0 that the not negation operator (or is it a modifier?) was added.

  4. Given a non-constrained generic method, like so:

    void Foo<T>( T x )
{
    if( x == null ) { DoSomething(); }

    DoSomethingElse();
}

    ...when the JIT instantiates the above generic method (i.e.: monomorphization) when T is a value-type (struct) then the entire if( x == null ) { DoSomething(); } statement (and its block contents) will be removed by the JIT compiler ("elision"), this is because a value-tupe can never be equal to null. While you'd expect that to be handled by any optimizing compiler, I understand that the .NET JIT has specially hardcoded rules for that particular scenario.

    • Curiously in earlier versions of C# (e.g. 7.0) the elision rule only applied to the == and != operators, but not the is operator, so while if( x == null ) { DoSomething(); } would be elided, the statement if( x is null ) { DoSometing(); } would not, and in fact you would get a compiler error unless T was constrained to where T : class. Since C# 8.0 this seems to now be allowed for unconstrained generic types.

  5. Surprisingly I couldn't find an authoritative source on this (as the published C# specs are now significantly outdated; and I don't want to go through the csc source-code to find out either).

    • If neither the C# compiler or JIT do apply impossible-branch-elision in generic code with Constant-pattern expressions then I think it might simply because it's too hard to do at-present.

  6. Note that a constant-expression does not mean a literal-expression: you can use named const values, enum members, and so on, even non-trivial raw expressions provided all sub-expressions are also constant-expressions.

    • I'm curious if there's any cases where static readonly fields could be used though.

  7. Note that in the case of typeof(X) != y.GetType(), this expression will return true when X is derived from y's type (as they are different types), but x is not Y is actually false because x is Y (because x is an instance of a subclass of Y). When using Type it's better to do something like typeof(X).IsSubclassOf(y.GetType()), or the even looser y.GetType().IsAssignableFrom(typeof(X)).

    • Though in this case, as Char is a struct and so cannot participate in a type-hierarchy, so doing !x.IsSubclassOf(typeof(Char)) would just be silly.

  8. Brackets are necessary to get the expected behavior in x is not (1 or 2 or 3) because without brackets the expression translates to x is (not 1) or (2) or (3). When x = 2 this would return true when most people understand the intent of the expression to be that x should be none of the values 1, 2, 3.

    • The syntax x is not 1 and not 2 and not 3 is also possible and would yield the same expected result, but is more verbose in most cases.

Q: Which API's are best for E-commerce Website? A:

Honestly, you can completely ignore SOAP

For you, the real choice is between REST and GraphQL.

  • REST is your safest bet. It’s standard, easy to debug, and handles traffic perfectly fine if you structure your database well.

  • GraphQL is technically the "best" for e-commerce (used by Shopify) because it lets you grab complex data (like products + reviews + images) in a single request.

Stick with REST.
